title: Climb anyway (Leviticus Rabbah 29:2)
hookLine: Jacob sees the nations' angels climb and fall, and fears to climb
tomorrow: why would God speak from a scraggly thorn bush?

cards: Watching other people fall teaches its own lesson. A friend's big plan folds. A cousin's move across the country goes bad.
You start to think: why try? Jacob, asleep on that stone, dreams of "a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven; and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it."
Leviticus Rabbah says he watched who climbed, and who came down.

teach.b: In this midrash, the angels are the guardian princes of great empires. One climbs a long way, and comes down. Another climbs, and comes down.
Then the Holy One says to Jacob: you, climb. And Jacob is afraid.
Will I come down like them? The midrash lets two voices speak. Jacob's first.
I've just watched every climber fall. Caution isn't cowardice; it's evidence. Who climbs a ladder that throws everyone off?
His case is honest about what he saw. Then God's. You aren't them.
Rabbi Meir says it with a sting: had you believed and climbed, you would never have come down. Fear kept the ladder empty. And the midrash doesn't leave Jacob there.
He asks: then will my children be stuck down here forever?
God answers with words from Jeremiah: fear not, Jacob My servant. Both voices are inside the text.
The careful one, who learns from falls. The daring one, who says your path isn't theirs. The midrash gives God the last word, and the last word is gentle.

how: Leviticus Rabbah 29:2 is studied around Rosh Hashanah, since the chapter is tied to the festival's Torah reading; Jacob's ladder itself is read with the portion Vayetze.

o: stay put; whoever climbs high is sure to fall
climbing is only for angels, not for people
take the step up, even after watching others fall

games.q: who says what on the ladder — tap the pairs.
p: afraid he'll come down like them
had you climbed, you'd not come down

s: in the midrash, Jacob climbs the ladder bravely
he's afraid and doesn't climb; the midrash names the cost.
in this midrash the climbing angels stand for empires
their princes climb and come down, one after another.
God ends the story angry at Jacob
the last word is Jeremiah's: fear not.

games.q: your friend won't try out for the play because everyone she knows got cut. give Jacob's best case, then God's.
o: Jacob: falls are evidence. God: you aren't them; climb anyway.
Jacob: she's lazy. God: try harder or you'll be punished.
Jacob: never risk anything. God: it doesn't matter either way.
games.why: the midrash lets both speak: Jacob's fear is honest; God's answer is fear not.

practice: Stand, if you can, feet together. Slowly rise onto your toes, the smallest climb there is, hold it while it's steady, then come down gently and rise again. Each time you rise, name one step you've been afraid to take.
If standing doesn't work for you, lift your chin and shoulders instead.

wordCard.voice: Climb anyway: God's word to Jacob in Leviticus Rabbah, after he watched others fall. The text answers fear with fear not.

orig.note: Hebrew: ladder, the one Jacob dreams of in Genesis 28:12.

carryVoice: For the road: climb anyway, since other people's falls aren't your ladder. Day fifteen seventy-eight.
